data.title: The Iran War Could Permanently Slash Reliance on Hormuz, IEA Says
data.description:
(05:00 GMT) *Confidence in Strait of Hormuz Has Been Shattered During Iran War, IEA Says
(05:00 GMT) *IEA: Middle East Set to Remain Cornerstone of Global Oil, Gas Supply
(05:00 GMT) The Iran War Could Permanently Slash Reliance on Hormuz, IEA Says

By Giulia Petroni

Shipping disruptions due to the Iran war have shattered confidence in the Strait of Hormuz, spurring a costly overhaul of the global energy trade that could dramatically cut the world's dependence on the route over the next decade, the International Energy Agency said.

Before the conflict, around 20 million barrels of oil a day passed through Hormuz, a narrow waterway connecting the Persian Gulf to global markets. That could fall to 8.5 million barrels a day by 2030 and to less than 2 million by 2035 if the strait remains severely disrupted, the Paris-based agency said in its World Energy Outlook.

"The Hormuz crisis has delivered a huge shock to the system," IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said. "I don't see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before."

Still, the Middle East is set to remain the world's largest exporter of oil to international markets as major Gulf producers race to build alternative pipelines and routes.

Since the Iran war began in late February, Saudi Arabia has relied on its East-West pipeline to move crude toward the Red Sea, while the United Arab Emirates used its pipeline to the port of Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman.

Now, around 7 million barrels a day of new pipeline capacity is under construction or under consideration to help Gulf producers move oil without passing through the strait, the IEA said. Building the projects will require an estimated $40 billion of investment, adding about $2 to the cost of each barrel of Middle Eastern oil exported, the agency estimates.

"It is not easy, but the energy world could conceivably manage without the strait," Birol said. "It cannot manage without the Middle East."

Meanwhile, global oil prices have been volatile: Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, swung from around $71 a barrel prewar to peaks above $126, before falling back toward $93 a barrel in November.

The price reaction was less severe than the scale of the disruption might have suggested, coinciding with a time of ample global supply and well-stocked inventories.

The IEA now expects the global oil market to swing back into oversupply as Middle Eastern production recovers faster than global demand growth. From a surplus of 1.7 million barrels a day in the current quarter, the glut is set to widen further next year to about 3.8 million barrels a day.

Between March and October, global oil demand fell by around 3.7 million barrels a day from a year earlier, as higher prices, physical shortages, government-imposed measures and weaker economic activity curbed consumption.

The decline was particularly sharp in the Middle East, where demand dropped 10%, and Asia, where it fell 5%. China's seaborne crude imports fell to around 6 million barrels a day in June from 11.6 million in February as the country drew down inventories, restricted fuel exports and switched between fuels.

Over time, the IEA also expects the crisis to reinforce a broader shift toward countries' domestic energy sources. Renewables and nuclear energy will be the biggest beneficiaries, while energy-efficiency measures, biofuels and, in some Asian countries, coal could also gain ground.

"All in all, countries want to rely more and more on homegrown energy," Birol said.

Volatile fuel prices have reinforced the case for electrification. Global demand for electricity has grown faster than the world economy since 2019 and at twice the rate of overall energy demand, driven by electric vehicles, air conditioning, industrial motors, heat pumps and data centers. The IEA expects electricity demand to accelerate further through 2035, with electricity approaching 30% of final energy consumption across all scenarios.

In its World Energy Outlook, the IEA presents a series of possible scenarios rather than a single forecast.

Write to Giulia Petroni at giulia.petroni@wsj.com

data.title: Korean Entertainment Stocks Surge on Hopes of K-Pop's Return to China
data.description:
By Megan Cheah

Shares of South Korean entertainment companies rose sharply after Seoul's agreement with Beijing opened the door for China to potentially loosen rules barring major K-pop acts from performing in the country.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung and China's leader Xi Jinping on Wednesday signed a bilateral free-trade agreement on services and investment, covering sectors such as film, during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China.

The deal suggests that China could be warming up to ending its de facto ban on Korean pop culture, sparking a rally in entertainment stocks.

Kospi constituent Hybe, the company managing boy band BTS, advanced 13% on Thursday. Shares of entertainment and media company CJ ENM, listed on the smaller Kosdaq board, climbed 23%. Television-drama producer Studio Dragon's stock jumped 30%, while K-pop company SM Entertainment gained 10%.

China's informal ban, which Beijing has never officially acknowledged, was imposed in protest of Seoul's decision to deploy a U.S. missile defense system in 2016. Since then, Chinese television networks, streaming platforms and movie theaters had effectively shut out Korean content, while major K-pop acts were largely barred from staging large-scale concerts.

The free-trade agreement has "revived hopes that Beijing will ease its restrictions on Korean entertainment," said Hana Securities analysts Lee Ki-hoon and Kim Chae-hyun in a note. K-pop companies' earnings could rise by around 40% if China eventually allows K-pop concerts to resume, they wrote.

Studio Dragon looks set to be a more direct beneficiary of the South Korea-China deal. "Studio Dragon could earn additional revenue if Chinese streaming platforms...begin airing Korean dramas they have already licensed, triggering revenue-sharing payments," the analysts said.

  • Jihye Lee contributed to this article.

Write to Megan Cheah at megan.cheah@wsj.com

data.title: Energy-security response to Iran war could cut oil demand by 4% by 2035, IEA says
data.description:
Key points:
  • IEA includes new stress tests for markets if Hormuz disruption continues
  • Conflict has caused cumulative losses of 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 bcm of gas, IEA says
  • Countries turning to electrification for energy security
  • Cooling demand in buildings will surpass heating for first time

By Susanna Twidale

The Middle East conflict has caused the biggest disruption ever to global oil and gas trade and could cut world oil demand by more than 4% by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching measures in response, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Thursday.

Energy markets have been rattled this year by the conflict, which has curbed shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a route that typically carries about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies and is a key artery for Gulf exports.

"In my view, the energy world will never be the same again as it was before the Iran war," IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said in an interview alongside the release of the agency's World Energy Outlook 2026.

The conflict has resulted in cumulative losses of 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 billion cubic metres (bcm) of gas supplies from the Gulf, the Paris-based agency said.

The annual outlook includes a range of scenarios based on existing and proposed energy policies. This year it also examines how governments and markets could respond to prolonged disruption in Hormuz.

Under a new Additional Response Case (ARC), the IEA said energy security concerns could speed up electrification, energy-efficiency measures and efforts to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels.

In that case, global oil demand in 2035 is 4.4 million barrels per day lower than under the agency's Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS), which reflects governments' current policy intentions. Electric vehicles alone would displace more than 11 million bpd of oil demand.

Global oil demand falls to 97 million bpd in 2035 and 85 million bpd by 2050 under ARC, compared with just over 101 million bpd in 2035 under STEPS

Gas demand under ARC is more than 300 bcm lower than under STEPS.

ELECTRIFICATION GROWING

The report said electrification is now cost-competitive across large parts of transport, heating and industry, although inadequate grids, charging networks and power supplies could slow its rollout.

"Many countries are seeing electrification as a policy option for energy security. Instead of importing energy, they decided to build energy at home," Birol said.

Electricity's share of final energy consumption is projected to approach 30% globally under STEPS, up from about 23% today, as transport, heating and parts of industry switch away from fossil fuels.

Alongside data centres, rising demand for cooling is emerging as one of the strongest drivers of electricity consumption. For the first time, demand for cooling in buildings has exceeded demand for heating, the IEA said, as higher temperatures and rising incomes drive rapid growth in air-conditioner use.

data.title: Asian bonds attract biggest monthly foreign inflow in four months
data.description:
Asian bonds attracted their strongest foreign inflows in four months in October, as concerns over the sustainability of the AI-driven equity rally weighed on major technology stocks and boosted demand for relatively safer fixed-income assets.

Foreign investors bought a net $9.43 billion of bonds in South Korea, Malaysia, India, Indonesia and Thailand, the largest monthly inflow since June, largely reversing the $9.48 billion in net outflows recorded the previous month, according to data from regulators and bond market bodies.

The MSCI All Country Asia ex-Japan Index (.MISX00000PUS) fell 6.91% last month, its steepest decline since March, triggering nearly $50 billion in foreign outflows from emerging Asian equity markets.

"Foreign investors continued to reduce exposure to the region’s crowded technology-heavy equity markets while maintaining demand for regional bonds," said Khoon Goh, the head of Asia research at ANZ in a note last week.

South Korean bonds recorded net foreign inflows of $5.4 billion last month, after two successive months of net sales.

"The shifting AI narrative may well be the largest factor driving UST outperformance, with meaningful spillovers into JGBs and KTBs," Eugene Leow, senior rates strategist at DBS, said in a note earlier this month.

The 10-year US Treasury yield , however, has risen 12.5 basis points so far this month after hitting a two-month low of 4.859% earlier in the month. The 10-year South Korean Treasury yield remains down about 6.6 basis points for the month. Yields move inversely to prices.

Foreigners also snapped up a significant $1.78 billion worth of Malaysian bonds last month after about $436 million in net sales the prior month.

Last month, the Malaysian government raised its 2026 growth forecast for the second time this year, to a range of 4.8% to 5.3%, and projected that the fiscal deficit would narrow to 3.3% in 2027.

Indonesian, Indian and Thai bonds also saw foreign inflows last month of $900 million, $764 million and $584 million, respectively.

data.title: PhysicsWallah shares gain after FY30 growth blueprint; Motilal Oswal sees ₹200 target
data.description:
Shares of PhysicsWallahLtd. were trading around 3% higher on Thursday, November 19, after the edtech company outlined an ambitious growth roadmap for FY30 at its investor day, targeting revenue of ₹9,000-10,000 crore and an EBITDA margin of more than 20%.

The company's revenue target represents an increase from the ₹3,900 crore reported in FY26 and implies a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of at least 25% between FY27 and FY30.

PhysicsWallah also expects its online business to contribute around two-thirds of total revenue by FY30, with the offline segment accounting for the remaining one-third. In FY26, the revenue mix between online and offline businesses stood at 52:48.

The management's strategy is centred on scaling its existing online platform, expanding into adjacent learner categories, improving the profitability of its offline centres and developing artificial intelligence-led products.

The company aims to strengthen its position across India's education market, estimated at around $185 billion-$195 billion, through asset-light offerings spanning K-12 and post-K-12 segments.

What brokerages say on PhysicsWallah

HSBC has maintained a ‘Buy’ rating on PhysicsWallah, with a price target of ₹150. HSBC said the company's ambition to achieve revenue of ₹9,000-10,000 crore and an EBITDA margin of over 20% by FY30, with online operations expected to account for nearly two-thirds of revenue.

Motilal Oswal has a ‘Buy’ rating on the stock and a price target of ₹200. It said management's FY30 revenue ambition implies a consolidated revenue CAGR of at least 25% over FY27-FY30.

Motilal Oswal highlighted the company's focus on scaling its online business, expanding into adjacent learner categories, improving offline profitability and building AI-led products.

DAM Capital has a ‘Buy’ rating on PhysicsWallah, with a price target of ₹155. It said that the company's FY30 targets include revenue of ₹9,000-10,000 crore, a pre-Ind AS EBITDA margin of over 20% and an online revenue contribution of around two-thirds, compared with 52% in FY26.

The brokerage believes the margin target could be conservative, as it implies a pre-Ind AS adjusted EBITDA margin of around 25% for the online business in FY30, below its current run rate of 27%.

On the offline business, DAM Capital expects PhysicsWallah to moderate the pace of new centre additions to 15-30 annually, with greater emphasis on operating performance and quality.

The brokerage estimates online revenue and EBITDA to grow at CAGRs of 24% and 35%, respectively, between FY27 and FY29. For the offline business, it projects revenue growth of 15% over the same period, with adjusted EBITDA turning positive from a loss of ₹38 crore in FY27 to a profit of ₹169 crore in FY29.

data.title: Indonesia parliament passes asset forfeiture bill into law
data.description:
Indonesia's parliament approved a new asset forfeiture law in a plenary vote on Thursday, allowing authorities in certain cases to seize assets linked to corruption and other crimes without the need to first secure a criminal conviction.

  • Civil society organisations and protesters had long called for the law to be passed, arguing it would strengthen asset recovery efforts

  • The law aims to remedy limitations in state asset recovery, which was largely dependent on securing a criminal conviction first, said Rini Widyantini, bureaucratic reform minister

  • She said the new rules apply to perpetrators who flee, die, or suffer from permanent illness

  • Authorities may freeze and seize suspected criminal assets before a court decides whether they should be forfeited, according to a parliamentary presentation slide shown during the vote

  • The latest draft of the law was not immediately made public

  • Lawmakers had agreed that the non-conviction mechanism applies only to assets worth at least 1 billion rupiah ($54,885), state news agency Antara reported earlier this month

  • It also applies to crimes linked to corruption, narcotics, and certain fraud offences, including cryptocurrency and online gambling schemes, local media reported

  • The Legal Aid Institute of Indonesia, a non-government organisation, said on Wednesday that the legislation could help fight corruption and recover criminal proceeds

  • But it warned that it granted extensive powers to freeze, seize and manage assets without sufficiently strong safeguards against abuse

  • The organisation cited a November 16 draft of the bill, which Reuters could not immediately verify

($1 = 18,220 rupiah)

data.title: Australian dollar falls after weak jobs data, bonds rally on rate cut hopes
data.description:
The Australian dollar dropped on Thursday after a surprisingly weak jobs print had markets abandon any chance of further rate hikes and double down on bets for rate cuts next year, sparking a rally in bonds to three-month highs.

Data showed Australia's labour market turned decisively weaker in October, shedding jobs for a second straight month. The unemployment rate hit a five-year high of 4.9%, well ahead of the central bank's expectations, as five rate hikes this year to 4.85% worked to curb demand.

Swaps are no longer pricing in any risk of a rate rise from the Reserve Bank of Australia but are expecting lower rates in the second half of next year. A June rate cut is seen at 68%, while a move in August is about fully priced in. (0#AUDIRPR)

The Aussie fell 0.5% to $0.6679, marking the eighth straight session of declines as growing anxiety over the AI trade added to a global equity sell-off. It is closing in on key support at $0.6662, the lowest level this year.

Bonds rallied on the prospects of rate cuts, with three-year bond yields (AU3YT=RR) down 17 basis points to 4.612%, the lowest since August. Ten-year bond yields slumped 12 bps to 4.977%, also a three-month low.

"The RBA face an increasingly worse policy conundrum. Inflation is still way too high... However, the pace of deterioration in the housing market & now the labour market is worrying," said George Tharenou, chief economist at UBS.

"We now expect the first rate cut of -25bps in Aug-27 (was Nov-27). We also now except an easing cycle of -75bps (was -50bps), with the most likely timing additional -25bps rate cuts in Nov-27 & Feb-28."

The kiwi dollar steadied at $0.5494 after finishing little changed on Wednesday. It is perching dangerously close above $0.5485 and $0.5469, with a breach of those levels opening the way to lows last seen in 2009.

The Aussie also lost 0.6% to NZ$1.2156 , the lowest since early September and well off its recent 13-year peak of NZ$1.2601.

Anna Breman, Governor of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, said on Thursday inflation was elevated due to costly fuel and a weaker currency, but an uneven recovery has limited businesses' ability to pass on higher costs.

Swaps now imply a 78% probability that the RBNZ will raise interest rates by a quarter percentage point to 3%, with 80 basis points of tightening priced in by the end of next year. (0#NZDIRPR)

data.title: Thailand central bank chief proposes 1% to 3% inflation target for 2027
data.description:
Thailand's central bank chief is proposing keeping the inflation target range at 1% to 3% for 2027 and said on Thursday he saw no need for an interest rate change for now.

The central bank still expects 2026 economic growth of 2.4%, with third-quarter growth of 2.9% close to its 3.1% forecast, despite revisions to the manufacturing production index, Governor Vitai Ratanakorn told reporters.

  • Interest rates will be kept steady if the economic outlook remains as expected, but decisions will be data-dependent at each meeting, he said

  • The central bank last month left its key interest rate (THCBIR=ECI) unchanged at 1.00%, with the next rate review on December 23

  • The interest-rate differential with the US is only one factor affecting the baht as any Fed rate increase could put some weakening pressure on the currency, Vitai said

  • Dollar movements remain a key driver of the baht, which has weakened but remains in line with regional currencies and the central bank is closely monitoring it, he said

  • Vitai said it was too early to assess US curbs on advanced chip exports, but risks to exports and investment will be monitored

  • The central bank aims to boost SME loan growth next year, Vitai said
